cues.text: First, some notation. Only the numbers matter, not the letters. So we write the system as an augmented matrix: the coefficient matrix A, then a bar, then the right-hand-side column b.
Each row is one equation: we'll call them R one, R two and R three. Each column belongs to one variable, x, y and z, and the last column holds the constants.
We are allowed three elementary row operations. One: swap two rows. Two: multiply a row by a non-zero number k. Three: replace a row by itself plus c times another row.
Our goal is row echelon form, a staircase shape. The first non-zero entry in each row is called a pivot, and every entry below a pivot is zero.
By the end of this video, you'll be able to reduce a three by three system to echelon form, solve it by back-substitution, and explain why row operations never change the solution.
